sovereignty

SOV-rin-tee · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Sovereignty means supreme, independent power to govern oneself or a nation without control from any outside authority.

The small island nation guarded its sovereignty fiercely, refusing every offer of foreign aid that came with even a hint of control over its laws.

Example

By keeping every customer record on servers physically inside its own country, the software firm protected its data sovereignty, so that no foreign government or overseas cloud provider could ever compel access to that information under laws written elsewhere.

Here, sovereignty names the firm's supreme, independent power to govern its own data with no outside authority able to override that control. Notice how much stronger this is than a looser word like independence, which can be casual or personal (you might value your "independence" simply because you like doing things your own way). It is also sharper than jurisdiction, which only describes the scope of a legal authority — which court or country gets to make a ruling — not the ultimate, self-ruling power itself. Sovereignty is the top of the chain: the authority that answers to nothing above it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

self-rule: Self-rule means governing your own affairs instead of being ruled by outsiders — the plain, everyday phrase for the idea. Sovereignty is the formal legal term and the more absolute one: supreme authority that no outside power can override.

independence: Independence means freedom from outside control, and it stretches from nations to teenagers to freelancers. Sovereignty is narrower and stronger: a state's supreme legal and political authority — not merely being free of control, but answering to no higher power at all.

supremacy: Supremacy means holding the highest authority or power over others, and it can describe any kind of dominance — military, legal, even athletic. Sovereignty is supremacy of one specific kind: a state's supreme right to govern itself, free of any outside authority.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

subjugation: Being forced under the domination and control of another power — the direct opposite of holding supreme authority over oneself.

vassalage: The condition of a vassal — holding your lands and loyalty under a superior lord's authority, the feudal opposite of answering to no one above you.

Where it sits · how free from outside control — dependency → autonomy → sovereignty

dependency vs. sovereignty: A dependency is governed by others and makes almost none of its own rules, while a nation with sovereignty answers to no power above itself.

autonomy vs. sovereignty: Autonomy lets a region run some of its own affairs under a higher authority's shadow; sovereignty removes the shadow entirely — nothing outranks the self-ruling state.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sovereign

Root — sovereign: one who stands above (Latin super, 'above,' which passed through Late Latin superanus and Old French soverain; the -g- crept in later by false association with reign)

Suffix — -ty

Suffix — -ty: state or condition of; forms nouns (Latin -tas, via Old French -té)

Put it together

Put it together: Sovereign (one who stands above — Latin super, 'above,' which passed through Late Latin superanus, 'one standing above,' and wore down into Old French soverain; the -g- crept into the spelling centuries later through false association with reign — a happy accident, since a sovereign does reign) + -ty (the state or condition of): sovereignty is literally 'the condition of standing above' — supreme power that no outside authority can override.

Use the root in a new word: supreme

Use the root in a new word: supreme: The nation's supreme court stands above every lower court — the same Latin super, "above," at work.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / political / legal

Sovereignty is a formal word at home in law, government, and international relations. In everyday speech it sounds out of place — you would say you have "control" of your own schedule, not "sovereignty" over it. Writers do occasionally borrow it figuratively for effect (a chef's "sovereignty" over the kitchen), but that is a deliberate, elevated flourish, not casual usage.
